accesskeys: Duplicate access keys cause keyboard shortcuts to malfunction, leaving users unable to navigate the page effectively.
area-alt: Image map areas require descriptions so screen reader users know where these interactive 'hotspots' lead.
aria-allowed-attr: Using ARIA attributes that aren't supported by an element's role sends contradictory signals to assistive technology, causing unpredictable behavior.
aria-allowed-role: Assigning an inappropriate ARIA role to an element misleads assistive technology about what the element is and how it should behave.
aria-braille-equivalent: Braille-specific labels must have a standard text equivalent so users on non-braille devices still receive the same information.
aria-command-name: Buttons, links, and menu items built with ARIA must have a name so screen reader users know what action they perform before activating them.
aria-conditional-attr: Using ARIA attributes outside the conditions specified for a role sends misleading signals to assistive technology, breaking expected behavior.
aria-deprecated-role: Deprecated ARIA roles are no longer reliably supported by assistive technology, meaning the element's purpose may be misread or ignored entirely.
aria-dialog-name: Dialogs and alerts without names leave screen reader users disoriented — they've been thrust into a new context with no explanation of what it is or why it appeared.
aria-hidden-body: Hiding the entire document body from assistive technology makes every piece of content on the page invisible to screen reader users.
aria-hidden-focus: Hiding an element from screen readers while keeping it focusable creates a 'ghost' element that confuses keyboard users.
aria-input-field-name: Form fields built with ARIA must have a name so screen reader users know what information they are being asked to enter.
aria-meter-name: A meter widget without a name gives no context for what is being measured, making the value meaningless to screen reader users.
aria-progressbar-name: An unnamed progress bar leaves screen reader users with no way to understand what task is in progress or how far along it is.
aria-prohibited-attr: Applying ARIA attributes that are forbidden for an element's role corrupts the accessibility information assistive technology relies on.
aria-required-attr: ARIA roles require specific attributes to function correctly; omitting them leaves the element in a broken state that assistive technology cannot interpret.
aria-required-children: ARIA composite widgets rely on specific child roles to communicate structure; missing children break the relationship and confuse assistive technology.
aria-required-parent: ARIA child roles are only meaningful inside specific parent roles; orphaned children are treated as errors by assistive technology.
aria-roledescription: Applying a custom role description to an element without a valid role means assistive technology has no reliable way to announce what the element actually is.
aria-roles: Invalid ARIA role values are ignored or misinterpreted by assistive technology, stripping the element of its intended semantic meaning.
aria-text: When role="text" is used on elements that contain focusable children, screen readers may split the content into fragments, breaking the intended reading experience.
aria-toggle-field-name: Toggle controls like checkboxes and switches built with ARIA must have a name so screen reader users understand what they are turning on or off.
aria-tooltip-name: A tooltip without an accessible name provides no information when a screen reader user encounters it, defeating its purpose entirely.
aria-treeitem-name: Tree view items without names leave screen reader users unable to understand the structure or content of the tree they are navigating.
aria-valid-attr: Misspelled or invented ARIA attributes are silently ignored by assistive technology, meaning the intended accessibility enhancement never takes effect.
aria-valid-attr-value: Invalid ARIA attribute values are ignored or misread by assistive technology, breaking the semantic information the developer intended to convey.
audio-caption: Without captions, audio content is completely inaccessible to users who are deaf or hard of hearing.
autocomplete-valid: Correct autocomplete attributes allow browsers to automatically fill in personal information for users with motor impairments, saving them significant effort.
avoid-inline-spacing: Hardcoded inline spacing overrides user stylesheet adjustments, blocking users with dyslexia or low vision who depend on custom text spacing to read comfortably.
blink: Blinking content is a known seizure trigger for users with photosensitive epilepsy and is too distracting to be usable for anyone with attention or cognitive difficulties.
button-name: Buttons without text (like icon-only buttons) give screen reader users no indication of what clicking them will do.
bypass: Skip links allow keyboard users to jump past repetitive navigation and get straight to the main content, saving time and effort.
color-contrast: Text with low contrast is difficult for users with low vision or those in bright environments to read.
color-contrast-enhanced: Meeting the enhanced AAA contrast threshold ensures text is readable for users with more severe vision impairments who struggle with the standard AA minimum.
css-orientation-lock: Locking the display to one orientation prevents users who mount their device in a fixed position — a common accommodation for motor impairments — from using the page at all.
definition-list: Improperly structured definition lists break the relationship between terms and their definitions, making the content confusing for screen reader users.
dlitem: Definition terms and details placed outside a definition list lose their semantic meaning, leaving screen reader users with no context for how the items relate.
document-title: Without a page title, screen reader users and those using multiple browser tabs have no way to identify the page they are on without reading its full content.
duplicate-id: Duplicate IDs corrupt the document structure that assistive technology depends on to identify and navigate to specific elements.
duplicate-id-active: Duplicate IDs on buttons or links can cause assistive technology to skip elements or trigger the wrong action entirely.
duplicate-id-aria: When ARIA relationships reference duplicate IDs, assistive technology may connect labels to the wrong elements, scrambling the information presented to users.
empty-heading: Empty headings clutter the page structure for screen reader users, making it harder to find the actual content they need.
empty-table-header: Empty table headers leave screen reader users unable to understand what data the column or row contains, making the table difficult or impossible to interpret.
focus-order-semantics: Elements that receive focus should have roles that signal they are interactive; non-interactive elements in the tab order confuse keyboard users about what they can do.
focus-visible: A visible focus indicator is the 'mouse cursor' for keyboard users; without it, they cannot see which element they are currently on.
form-field-multiple-labels: Multiple labels on a single form field cause screen readers to announce conflicting or redundant information, making it unclear what the field is asking for.
frame-focusable-content: Setting tabindex=-1 on a frame with focusable content traps keyboard users outside the frame, making any interactive elements inside it unreachable.
frame-tested: Untested frames may contain accessibility violations that are invisible to the audit, leaving users with an incomplete picture of the page's actual accessibility.
frame-title: Frames require names so users navigating via assistive technology can identify the purpose of the embedded content.
frame-title-unique: Frames with identical titles are indistinguishable from each other, leaving screen reader users unable to choose the correct frame to enter.
heading-order: A logical heading hierarchy (H1, then H2, etc.) acts as a table of contents, helping users build a mental map of the page.
hidden-content: Hidden content may contain accessibility violations that affect users when the content becomes visible, and should be reviewed even if not currently displayed.
html-has-lang: Setting a language allows screen readers to use the correct accent and pronunciation, preventing the content from sounding like gibberish.
html-lang-valid: An invalid language code causes screen readers to load the wrong voice profile, making the content difficult or impossible to understand.
html-xml-lang-mismatch: Conflicting lang and xml:lang attributes send contradictory language signals to assistive technology, causing unpredictable pronunciation behavior.
identical-links-same-purpose: Links with the same visible label that go to different destinations create confusion for all users, particularly those who use link lists to navigate.
image-alt: Screen reader users rely on text descriptions to understand the meaning, context, and purpose of images.
image-redundant-alt: Repeating the same text in an image description and an adjacent caption creates a repetitive and annoying experience for screen reader users.
input-button-name: Submit and reset buttons without discernible text leave screen reader users unable to identify the button's function before activating it.
input-image-alt: Image-based buttons require alternative text so users know the function of the button (e.g., 'Search' or 'Submit').
label: Form fields without labels are inaccessible to screen reader users and make it impossible for them to know what data to enter.
label-content-name-mismatch: When a button or link's visible text doesn't match its accessible name, voice control users who speak the visible text aloud cannot activate the element.
label-title-only: Labels conveyed only through tooltips or title attributes are invisible to keyboard-only users who never hover, effectively hiding the form field's purpose from them.
landmark-banner-is-top-level: The banner (header) should be a direct child of the document. Nesting it inside other areas makes it harder for users to locate the site's global branding and search.
landmark-complementary-is-top-level: Aside elements nested inside other landmarks may be misidentified by assistive technology, making supplementary content harder to find and understand.
landmark-contentinfo-is-top-level: The contentinfo (footer) landmark provides essential metadata and contact info; nesting it inside other sections can hide it from structural navigation tools.
landmark-main-is-top-level: Nesting the main landmark inside another landmark confuses assistive technology about where the primary content begins and ends.
landmark-no-duplicate-banner: Multiple banner landmarks confuse screen reader users about which area contains the site's primary header and global navigation.
landmark-no-duplicate-contentinfo: Multiple contentinfo landmarks make it ambiguous which area contains the site's footer information, disorienting users who rely on landmark navigation.
landmark-no-duplicate-main: A page should only have one primary content area. Multiple 'main' landmarks confuse screen reader users who use them to jump straight to the unique content of a page.
landmark-one-main: Without a 'main' landmark, users navigating via assistive technology have no quick way to bypass navigation menus and get straight to the primary content.
landmark-unique: Identical landmarks with no distinguishing label are indistinguishable from each other, leaving screen reader users unable to choose the correct section to navigate to.
link-in-text-block: Links that are only differentiated from surrounding text by color are invisible to users who are colorblind, making those links impossible to identify.
link-name: Links need clear, unique text so users know exactly where a link goes before they decide to click it.
list: Proper list markup tells screen readers how many items are in a group, helping users understand the scale of the information provided.
listitem: List items placed outside a list element lose their semantic context, leaving screen reader users unable to understand that they are part of a group.
marquee: Scrolling marquee text moves too fast for many users to read and cannot be paused, making it inaccessible to users with cognitive or motor impairments.
meta-refresh: Automatic page redirects disorient users, especially screen reader users who may be mid-sentence when the page suddenly reloads or changes.
meta-refresh-no-exceptions: Any timed page refresh interrupts the user experience and can cause screen reader users to lose their place, with no exceptions permitted at the AAA level.
meta-viewport: Disabling pinch-to-zoom prevents users with low vision from enlarging text to a readable size, locking them out of the content.
meta-viewport-large: Restricting zoom to less than 500% prevents users with significant vision impairments from scaling text to a size they can read.
nested-interactive: Nesting interactive elements like buttons inside links creates ambiguous behavior that assistive technology handles inconsistently, causing confusion for users.
no-autoplay-audio: Audio that plays automatically without warning can disorient screen reader users, whose own audio output is suddenly competing with unexpected sound.
object-alt: Embedded objects without alternative text are completely invisible to screen reader users, hiding whatever content or functionality they provide.
p-as-heading: Paragraphs styled to look like headings are ignored by screen readers when building the page outline, breaking navigation for users who rely on heading structure.
page-has-heading-one: A page without an H1 heading gives screen reader users no clear entry point into the content and makes the page structure harder to understand.
presentation-role-conflict: Elements marked as presentational that still have focusable behavior or ARIA attributes send contradictory signals that different screen readers handle inconsistently.
region: Landmarks (like 'nav' or 'main') allow users to skip directly to specific sections of the page without having to tab through everything else.
role-img-alt: Elements with an image role but no alternative text are announced as images by screen readers with no description, leaving users with no idea what they contain.
scope-attr-valid: Incorrect scope attributes on table headers break the association between headers and their data cells, making complex tables impossible to understand for screen reader users.
scrollable-region-focusable: If a scrolling box isn't focusable, keyboard users can't scroll through the content, effectively 'locking' it away from them.
select-name: Dropdown menus without names prevent screen reader users from knowing what selection they are being asked to make.
server-side-image-map: Server-side image maps require a mouse to activate specific regions, making them completely inaccessible to keyboard and screen reader users.
skip-link: A skip link that points to a non-existent or non-focusable target does nothing, leaving keyboard users to tab through the entire navigation on every page.
summary-name: A summary element without discernible text gives keyboard and screen reader users no indication of what content the disclosure widget contains before they expand it.
svg-img-alt: SVG images used as meaningful content require alternative text so screen reader users understand what the graphic represents.
tabindex: Using a tabindex greater than 0 disrupts the natural navigation flow, making the page unpredictable and frustrating for keyboard users.
table-duplicate-name: When a table's caption and summary contain identical text, screen reader users hear the same information announced twice, which is redundant and confusing.
table-fake-caption: Using a data cell to visually caption a table breaks the programmatic structure, causing screen readers to treat the caption as ordinary data rather than a table title.
target-size: Touch targets that are too small or too close together are difficult to activate accurately for users with tremors, limited dexterity, or large fingers.
td-has-header: Data cells in large tables without associated headers leave screen reader users unable to understand what category or dimension the cell's value belongs to.
td-headers-attr: Headers attributes that reference cells outside the table or non-header cells produce incorrect associations that mislead screen reader users about the data.
th-has-data-cells: Table headers that don't correspond to any data cells indicate broken table structure, which confuses screen reader users trying to make sense of the data.
valid-lang: Using an invalid language code prevents screen readers from loading the correct voice profile for that specific language.
video-caption: Without captions, video content is completely inaccessible to users who are deaf or hard of hearing, and difficult to follow in noisy or quiet environments.
